bridge: Builds on C06 operating-system boundaries and L03 reproducibility. Choose the linked platform setup appropriate to your computer; a container is not a replacement for every VM boundary.
teaching:
A VM is like a separate practice computer running inside your computer. Its operating system is the guest; your physical computer is the host. The hypervisor is the software layer providing virtual hardware. RAM is working memory, virtual disk is saved storage, and a network interface connects the guest to selected networks. A container is closer to giving a program its own view of folders and processes while using the engine host’s operating-system kernel. These analogies explain the arrangement, not a promise of perfect containment.

A virtual machine runs a guest operating system behind a hypervisor boundary. A container usually shares its host kernel while isolating selected resources and namespaces. These different trust models matter when choosing where to run unfamiliar software. A container configured with excessive host access can undermine its intended boundary.

A snapshot records a recoverable state under the tool's rules. It is not automatically an independent backup and may include sensitive data. Keep a clean baseline, record network mode and define how to restore it before starting a lab. Disable unnecessary shared folders, credentials and exposed services.

A reproducible lab record states host/guest versions, allocated resources, image provenance, network configuration and expected observations. Verify isolation with harmless checks: an intentionally local training server should not listen on every interface. Do not infer total containment from one successful test. Where hardware cannot support the required platform, use the provider's designated training environment rather than improvising on a shared production device.

For Linux containers, namespaces separate views of resources, cgroups account for and limit selected resources, and capabilities/seccomp/security policy restrict selected operations. None alone proves containment. Containers share the engine host’s kernel; on Docker Desktop that engine commonly lives in a Linux VM. A Docker-daemon handle can grant substantial host authority even when the application runs as a non-root user. A VM normally has its own guest kernel; hosted and bare-metal hypervisors have different surrounding trust requirements. A language virtual machine is another abstraction again. Explicit shared folders, ports, clipboard/agent channels, credentials and external services remain boundaries to review. Restoring a VM snapshot does not undo writes already sent to those external resources.
example:
Lab plan (paper fixture)
Host: your own computer
Guest: supported training Linux VM
Network: NAT or isolated mode chosen for the exercise
Shared folders: none initially
Credentials: invented lab-only values
Baseline: clean-setup snapshot
Recovery check: create marker.txt, restore baseline, confirm marker absent
Exposed app: loopback only unless the lab explicitly requires otherwise
explanation: The marker test checks restoration behaviour without introducing hostile software. It does not prove that every disk or external volume is covered by the snapshot. Record which state is excluded. NAT connectivity is not an automatic assurance that all traffic or inbound access is forbidden.
exercise: Produce the full lab plan above for your selected platform. If a supported VM is available, perform the harmless marker restore. Otherwise complete the paper plan and explicitly label the runtime restore check unperformed; do not mark it as verified.
solution: Example paper plan: supported Linux guest from the training provider’s official image; record exact image version and download source; allocate RAM/disk within that platform’s documented requirements and your available capacity; choose an isolated lab network; no shared folders, clipboard sharing or personal credentials; name the clean snapshot baseline. Create marker.txt inside the guest, restore baseline, and record whether the marker disappeared if you actually perform the test. List excluded external disks/services. If no VM is available, label the entire restore observation unperformed and retain the completed paper design.
challenge: Compare two proposed labs: A mounts your entire home directory writable into a container; B uses a clean VM with no shared folders and invented data. Explain the extra exposure in A and propose a minimal change.
challenge_solution: A grants access to unrelated personal files and expands consequences of a compromised process. Remove the broad mount, share only an explicit disposable directory if needed and choose a VM boundary for workloads that require it. Neither configuration is a universal containment guarantee.
